metadata.title: Adolescents want to be teachers? Affecting factors and two-decade trends in 39 educational systems

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA microdata from the 2000 and 2018 cycles for 15-year-olds, restricting analyses to the 39 economies where both cycles’ teaching-expectation data were available. It applies appropriate survey weights at each level of analysis (student and school) to account for PISA’s two-stage stratified sampling design (schools sampled first, then students within schools) and to support representativeness within each economy. The manuscript does not report the exact weight variable names (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly states that survey weights were incorporated at each level. Because the models are multilevel logistic regressions rather than ML algorithms, the weighting is treated as part of the complex-survey estimation strategy rather than an ML-specific preprocessing step.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses PISA 2000 and PISA 2018 data for 15-year-olds and examines two-decade trends in teaching-career expectations using only the 39 economies for which teaching-expectation data were available in both cycles. The outcome is restricted to students who provided an expectation about their future job and whose coded occupation corresponds to teaching (primary, secondary, or special education teachers), which is then recoded dichotomously (expected teaching vs not). Predictors are drawn from variables available across the two cycles (e.g., ESCS, reading achievement, math/science achievement, enjoyment of reading, self-efficacy, parents’ teaching careers, family support, teacher support), with teacher enthusiasm included only for 2018. Missing values in predictors are handled via multiple imputation, and the models include school-level controls (school mean ESCS and school mean academic achievement) plus student-level predictors with group-mean centering at the school level.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000 & 2018 (15-year-olds), Reading and MS achievement (combined) — 39 economies
main_findings.target_variable: Teaching career expectation (dichotomous: expected teacher vs not)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel logistic regression; predicted probabilities (Pr) reported by gender and economy; no AUC/RMSE/accuracy reported.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000 and 2018 data for 15-year-olds across 39 economies, the study leveraged gender, ESCS, reading achievement, math/science achievement, and enjoyment of reading to predict whether students expected to become teachers, finding that the overall proportion expecting teaching declined from 2000 to 2018 (average 4.8% to 4.3%) while boys’ and girls’ associations with predictors varied by economy and time. This indicates that teacher-workforce recruitment policies should be tailored by gender and local context, with particular attention to reading enjoyment and supportive learning environments rather than relying on a single uniform driver.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes two-decade trends in adolescents’ expectations to become teachers using OECD PISA microdata from 2000 and 2018 for 15-year-olds, focusing on 39 economies where teaching-expectation data were available in both cycles. The outcome is an open-ended ISCO-coded job expectation recoded dichotomously (expected teacher vs not), and predictors include ESCS, reading achievement, a combined math/science achievement measure (MS), enjoyment of reading, self-efficacy, parents’ teaching careers, family support, teacher support, and teacher enthusiasm (2018 only). The authors estimate multilevel logistic regression models with school-level random effects, apply multiple imputation for missing predictors, and use all plausible values for achievement outcomes combined via Rubin’s rules. They report predicted probabilities (Pr) and descriptive trend percentages rather than ML metrics (e.g., AUC/RMSE), and the paper does not train ML algorithms; therefore, results are predictive associations and cannot establish causality.
